summary.text: For an arbitrary bound \(B\), apply the assumed representation to \(n=(B+6)!\), obtaining primes \(p=6x-1\) and \(q=6y+1\) with \(p+q=6n\). If either the Sophie Germain prime \(p\), or the lower twin prime \(q-2\), were at most \(B\), the corresponding bounded prime would divide \(n\) and hence divide the other prime; primality would force equality, contradicting the strict inequality between them coming from the factorial’s size, so both families are unbounded and therefore infinite.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
S=\{p\in\mathbb N: p\text{ is prime and }2p+1\text{ is prime}\}
\]
be the set of Sophie Germain primes, and let
\[
T=\{q\in\mathbb N:q\text{ is prime and }q+2\text{ is prime}\}
\]
be the set of smaller members of twin-prime pairs.

For an integer \(n\), the number \(a(n)=A227923(n)\) is the sum, over all integers \(x\) with \(1\le x<n\), of an indicator which is \(1\) precisely when, on putting \(y=n-x\), all four numbers
\[
6x-1,\qquad 12x-1,\qquad 6y-1,\qquad 6y+1
\]
are prime, and is \(0\) otherwise.

Assume that
\[
a(n)>0\qquad\text{for every }n>1.
\]
We first record the immediate consequence of this assumption that will be used twice. For every \(n>1\), there are integers \(x,y\ge 1\) such that
\[
x+y=n
\]
and
\[
6x-1,\quad 12x-1,\quad 6y-1,\quad 6y+1
\]
are all prime. Indeed, the defining sum for \(a(n)\) is a finite sum of zeros and ones. If it is positive, at least one summand is \(1\). Its index \(x\) satisfies \(1\le x<n\), so \(y=n-x\ge1\), and the fact that this summand is \(1\) gives exactly the four asserted primality conditions.

For such a representation, introduce the notation
\[
P=6x-1,\qquad Q=6y-1,\qquad R=6y+1.
\]
Because \(x,y\ge1\), the subtractions in these expressions cause no exceptional behavior. We have
\[
2P+1=2(6x-1)+1=12x-1,
\]
so \(P\) is a Sophie Germain prime. Also
\[
Q+2=(6y-1)+2=6y+1=R,
\]
so \(Q\) is the smaller member of a twin-prime pair. Finally, the relation \(x+y=n\) gives the central identity
\[
P+R=(6x-1)+(6y+1)=6(x+y)=6n. \tag{1}
\]

We will prove separately that \(S\) and \(T\) contain elements larger than every prescribed bound. A set of natural numbers with this property is infinite: if it were finite, its elements would have a maximum, contradicting the existence of an element larger than that maximum.

First consider the Sophie Germain primes. Let \(B\) be an arbitrary nonnegative integer. Set
\[
m=B+6,
\qquad
n=m!.
\]
Since \(m\ge6\), we have \(n=m!>1\), and also \(m\le m! = n\). Apply the representation established above to this value of \(n\). Thus there are positive \(x,y\) with \(x+y=n\), with all four associated numbers prime. In particular, \(P=6x-1\) belongs to \(S\).

We claim that \(P>B\). Suppose, for a contradiction, that
\[
P=6x-1\le B. \tag{2}
\]
Then \(P\le B<m=B+6\). Since \(P\) is prime, it is positive; and every positive integer at most \(m\) divides \(m!\). Consequently
\[
P\mid m!=n,
\]
and hence also
\[
P\mid 6n. \tag{3}
\]
On the other hand, \(P\) plainly divides itself. Subtracting \(P\) from the identity (1), or equivalently using \(R=6n-P\), equations (1) and (3) therefore imply
\[
P\mid R. \tag{4}
\]

Because \(R=6y+1\) is prime, every positive divisor of \(R\) is either \(1\) or \(R\). Thus (4) leaves precisely two cases:
\[
P=1 \quad\text{or}\quad P=R. \tag{5}
\]
The first case is impossible because \(P\) is prime and no prime equals \(1\). To exclude the second case, we derive a strict inequality.

From (2), and from \(x\ge1\), we obtain
\[
6x\le B+1.
\]
In particular,
\[
2x\le 6x\le B+1<B+6=m\le n.
\]
Thus \(2x<n\). Since \(y=n-x\), this says
\[
x< n-x=y.
\]
It follows that
\[
P=6x-1<6y+1=R.
\]
Hence \(P\ne R\), excluding the second case in (5) as well. This contradiction proves \(P>B\).

Since \(B\) was arbitrary, for every bound \(B\) there is a Sophie Germain prime \(P>B\). Therefore the set \(S\) of Sophie Germain primes is infinite.

We now prove the infinitude of twin-prime pairs. Again let \(B\) be an arbitrary nonnegative integer, and again set
\[
m=B+6,
\qquad
n=m!.
\]
As before, \(n>1\), so the hypothesis supplies positive integers \(x,y\) with \(x+y=n\) for which \(P=6x-1\), \(12x-1\), \(Q=6y-1\), and \(R=6y+1\) are prime. Since \(R=Q+2\), the number \(Q\) belongs to \(T\).

We claim that \(Q>B\). Suppose instead that
\[
Q=6y-1\le B. \tag{6}
\]
Then
\[
R=Q+2\le B+2\le B+6=m.
\]
The number \(R\) is prime and therefore positive. Since every positive integer at most \(m\) divides \(m!\), it follows that
\[
R\mid m!=n,
\]
and hence
\[
R\mid 6n. \tag{7}
\]
Using the identity \(P+R=6n\), and subtracting the divisible summand \(R\), we conclude from (7) that
\[
R\mid P. \tag{8}
\]

The number \(P\) is prime. Therefore its positive divisor \(R\) must satisfy one of the two alternatives
\[
R=1 \quad\text{or}\quad R=P. \tag{9}
\]
The first is impossible because \(R\) is itself prime. We rule out the second by showing that in fact \(R<P\).

From (6) we have
\[
6y\le B+1.
\]
Consequently
\[
2y\le6y\le B+1<B+6=m\le n.
\]
Thus \(2y<n\). Since \(x=n-y\), this gives
\[
y<n-y=x.
\]
As \(x\) and \(y\) are integers, \(x\ge y+1\), and therefore
\[
P=6x-1\ge 6(y+1)-1=6y+5>6y+1=R.
\]
Hence \(R\ne P\), contradicting the only remaining alternative in (9). The supposition (6) is therefore false, and \(Q>B\).

Thus for every bound \(B\), there is a twin-prime representative \(Q>B\), meaning that both \(Q\) and \(Q+2\) are prime. Hence \(T\) is infinite. Since distinct smaller representatives determine distinct twin-prime pairs, there are infinitely many twin-prime pairs.

We have proved both conclusions: the positivity of \(A227923(n)\) for every integer \(n>1\) implies that there are infinitely many Sophie Germain primes and infinitely many twin-prime pairs.
